source_title_hint: How To Fix Your Rounded Shoulders Posture
primary_summary: The video explains that shoulder blade (scapular) winging and rounded shoulders are often caused by asymmetrical torso rotation and rib‑cage compression on one side, which restricts scapular glide. It recommends expanding the compressed side of the ribcage and using a wall‑supported hip‑knee‑bent exercise to improve rib‑cage mobility and reposition the scapula.

classification.usefulness_reason: Provides clear biomechanical explanation and a concise corrective exercise

problem_statements: Winged scapula on one side due to compressed ribcage and torso rotation
Rounded shoulders resulting from limited rib‑cage expansion on the compressed side
key_visual_points: Winged scapula visible when turning to the right
Ribcage compression on the right side pulls sternum leftward
Exercise performed with hips/knees at ~90° and back 1 inch from wall
exercises_mentioned: Hip‑knee bent wall‑support rib‑cage expansion exercise
advice_mentioned: Expand the ribcage on the compressed side during inhalation
Use muscles to reposition the scapula on the back ribcage

knowledge_units.title: Scapular winging originates from asymmetrical rib‑cage compression
knowledge_units.summary: When the torso rotates toward one side, the ribcage on that side becomes compressed and depressed, pulling the sternum and limiting scapular glide. This causes the opposite scapula to wing and the shoulder to round forward.
observable_signs: Visible winging of one shoulder blade when turning to the side
Rounded forward posture of the shoulder on the compressed side
mechanisms: Compressed ribcage pulls sternum toward the rotated side
Scapula cannot glide/rotate effectively on a compressed ribcage
when_useful: Assessing patients with unilateral shoulder winging
when_not_useful: Symmetrical postural deviations without ribcage involvement

knowledge_units.title: Wall‑supported hip‑knee bent rib‑cage expansion exercise
knowledge_units.summary: Position with hips and knees bent ~90°, back one inch from the wall; inhale to expand the ribcage on the compressed side, using muscles to reposition the scapula for better glide.
execution_steps: Sit or kneel with hips and knees flexed to approximately 90°
Place your back about one inch away from a wall to provide tactile feedback
Inhale deeply, feeling the ribcage expand on the side that is usually compressed
Engage the muscles around the scapula to gently pull it onto the back of the ribcage
cues: Keep back close (≈1 in) to the wall
Feel ribcage expansion on the compressed side during inhalation
breathing_cues: Inhale to expand the ribcage fully on both sides
errors_to_avoid: Arching the lower back away from the wall
when_useful: When scapular winging is linked to ribcage compression
when_not_useful: If ribcage compression is not present
